newsitem.title: UK: Sugar-Latam producers muscle into EU export market.
newsitem.headline: Sugar-Latam producers muscle into EU export market.

text.p: European Union (EU) sugar premiums are staying low as producers wait for higher prices and the steady trickle of Middle East demand is satisfied by cheaper suppliers, brokers said on Friday.
Premiums were quoted at between $2 and $4 over spot futures for nearby shipment periods but producers were likely to fight hard to achieve higher prices, they said.

"They (producers) are not dropping their prices -- if you paid $3 they'd probably back away and you might get business at a $5 premium and a little bit more for further forward shipment," said one physical trader.
"They're holding back rather than seeing any offers pushing the market down. But equally the buyers don't want to pay up unless they have to and are looking for alternative sugars," he said.
While availability of EU cargoes is reported to be generally good, producers are facing increased competition for same-quality sugars from countries such as Mexico and Guatemala.

Yemen featured recently on the freight market to take bagged cargoes from both countries. However, inquiry has also been seen for Spanish sugar to be shipped to Iran and Syria and for French sugar to Iraq.
Iran is expected to continue its steady stream of white sugar imports until the summer at a rate of around three cargoes a month.
The EU also faces competition from the region's new and planned refineries, particularly Dubai's Al Khaleej plant at Jebel Ali which has an annual capacity of 720,000 tonnes.
"There's plenty of availability of 45 (ICUMSA sugar) in the EU. The main market was the Middle East and that's now being fed quite well with Al Khaleej sugar," one broker said.
"But I doubt that when we get to August there will be a big carry-over -- in the end the EUs have been so cheap relatively that they will all disappear."

EU premiums were likely to erode further towards the summer with cargoes of 1996/97 crop sugar probably being traded at flat, unlike in previous years, he said. Physical market sources said interest was more in the raws, especially with the recent activity seen from central American origins before new crop Brazilian sugars become available.

Delivery against the expiry of New York's March contract was dominated by Guatemala and Mexico, with 971 lots of Guatemalans tendered, 551 lots of Mexicans and lesser amounts from Costa Rica and El Salvador.
According to official statistics, Guatemala's principal export destinations this year have been Ivory Coast, Chile, the United States, Haiti, Jamaica, Morocco, Mexico, Peru and Sri Lanka.
The question is now how much central American sugar remains before Brazil returns as a supplier.
"People are now wondering what's available for the May," the physical trader said.
"At the moment you're not getting any Brazils as there are none left over from the tail-end of the crop in the north and I don't think they can get anything out of the south," he said.
Some central American sugars had already been used instead of Cubans, which could present political problems for some traders or were subject to shipment delays.

In light of the reduction in western hemisphere supply -- excluding Cuba, which is prohibited from delivering sugar against the New York market -- Thailand would probably feature as a tendered origin against May.
"Maybe some of the Thai raws will have to be delivered because they're not finding all the markets they would like compared to previous years in the Far East," the trader said.
